title: Your AI Policy Is a Rule, and Students Route Around Rules
author: Doan Winkel
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), July 26, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel argues that a single-paragraph AI policy in a syllabus functions as a prohibition that students learn to route around rather than a framework that shapes how they learn. His alternative has two parts: first, design the workflow—specify at which step in an assignment AI may enter, ensuring students do the core cognitive work before using AI to challenge or pressure their thinking. Second, make honesty cheap by requiring a per-assignment disclosure sentence describing what tool was used, what was asked of it, and what the student did with the output. Structural insights include setting AI expectations per assignment rather than per course, and avoiding any policy that makes disclosure more costly than hiding, which simply teaches students that concealment is the smart move.
points: A prohibition-based AI policy teaches students where the lines are so they can navigate around them, not how to use AI in ways that actually build thinking.

The critical design principle: students should complete the core cognitive work first, then use AI to challenge, critique, or pressure-test their thinking—the same tool produces learning in one sequence and replaces it in another.

Part two of the framework is a minimal, per-assignment disclosure standard: tool name, what was asked, and what the student did with the output—a sentence that tells an instructor far more than 'AI used here.'
AI expectations belong on individual assignment sheets, not buried in a semester-long syllabus, because different assignments have genuinely different appropriate AI interactions.
Any policy that makes disclosure more costly than concealment has accidentally optimized for dishonesty; the disclosure standard should be cheap enough that students choose transparency by default.
quotes: A list of prohibitions teaches a student how to hide, not how to work.

A student who asks the bot to write the argument skips the exact struggle where learning lives. A student who writes the argument first and then asks the bot to attack it has to defend it or rethink it. It's the same tool, but one of those students got smarter.
So stop writing rules about AI and start writing the workflow. Do the thinking first, then let the machine pressure it.

A student who writes 'I used AI on this' has told you nothing. A student who writes 'I asked ChatGPT to outline counterarguments, then wrote and rejected two of them myself' has told you where she leaned and where she worked.
If honesty about AI use costs points, you have taught your class that hiding it is the correct strategy. They are very good at strategy.
Set it per assignment, not per course. 'AI allowed' across fifteen weeks means nothing when week three is a reflection and week eleven is a data analysis.
